rows.subtopic: Managing time in a heavy semester
rows.subtype: Approach: prioritising urgent versus important tasks [Thinking]
rows.description: Facing two assignments, a lab file and a club event in one week, the student sorts by deadline and marks, and drops the least valuable item.

rows.subtopic: Managing time in a heavy semester
rows.subtype: Approach: weekly schedule with time blocks [Action]
rows.description: On Sunday the student blocks classes, study slots, meals, gym and sleep in a calendar, and keeps buffer space for surprises.

rows.subtopic: Managing time in a heavy semester
rows.subtype: Approach: planning fallacy about assignment length [Pitfall]
rows.description: The student assumes a report will take two hours, starts late, and needs a whole night, and the same underestimate repeats every week.

rows.subtopic: Managing time in a heavy semester
rows.subtype: Approach: adding a buffer after past overruns [Revision]
rows.description: Having seen that tasks took about double, the student multiplies estimates by one and a half and starts earlier, and deadlines stop being panics.

rows.subtype: Approach: implementation intention with a fixed cue [Thinking]
rows.description: The young professional decides: after I brush my teeth in the morning, I walk for 20 minutes. Linking the habit to an existing routine removes the daily decision.

rows.subtype: Approach: start with a tiny version that can be done on bad days [Action]
rows.description: The person begins with ten minutes of stretching and a short jog rather than a one-hour gym session, and adds time each week. Small steps build consistency before intensity.

rows.subtype: Approach: all-or-nothing plan with a five-day-a-week gym [Pitfall]
rows.description: Motivated on 1 January, the person signs up for a year and plans daily hard workouts. A cold and a busy week break the streak, and the person drops the whole plan feeling like a failure.

rows.subtype: Approach: track and adjust after a missed week [Revision]
rows.description: After missing a week, the person does not scrap the plan but notes that late evenings fail and moves sessions to mornings, with a rule of never missing twice in a row. Treating a lapse as data keeps the habit alive.

rows.subtype: Approach: working backward from the exam date [Thinking]
rows.description: A candidate counts weeks to the exam, subtracts revision and mock periods, and sees how many days are left for each syllabus block, which shows that the plan needs a cut.

rows.subtype: Approach: prioritising by marks weightage [Thinking]
rows.description: Analysing past papers, the aspirant sees which topics carry the most marks and starts with those, leaving rarely asked topics for the end.

rows.subtype: Approach: collecting resources instead of studying [Pitfall]
rows.description: The candidate joins many groups, downloads dozens of PDFs and switches teachers, feeling busy, but never finishes one book, so there is little retention.

rows.subtype: Approach: emotion-aware planning for slumps [Revision]
rows.description: Noticing that scores dip after sleepless weeks, the aspirant adds fixed sleep, a short evening walk and one free evening weekly, and finds accuracy improving.

rows.subtype: Approach: copying a peer [Action]
rows.description: A child watches another child join a group by asking, "Can I play too?" and repeats the same words the next day at the sandpit, with a smile.

rows.subtype: Approach: bargaining [Action]
rows.description: A child offers a friend the first turn on the new bicycle in return for playing tag afterwards. Trading what the friend wants for what the child wants opens the play.

rows.subtype: Approach: bossing [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child says, "You have to play my game or I won't be your friend," and the other child walks away. Demanding works less well than offering.

rows.subtype: Approach: task decomposition into a packing and route list [Action]
rows.description: A girl helps plan a visit to her grandparents by listing tasks: book tickets, pack clothes, arrange food for the train, and tick them off with her mother the week before.

rows.subtype: Approach: comparing travel options by cost and comfort [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy compares train, bus and car for a trip to Agra, noting the train is cheaper and safer at night while the car allows stops, and helps the family choose the train.

rows.subtype: Approach: making a wish list without limits [Pitfall]
rows.description: The child suggests visiting six places in two days, and only when his father points at the map and clock does he see that travel time makes the plan impossible.

rows.subtype: Approach: adjusting the plan to fit the budget [Revision]
rows.description: After learning the family can spend only ten thousand rupees, the girl removes the water park and keeps the fort and museum, which cost less and everyone still enjoys.

rows.subtype: Approach: using the caregiver as a tool [Action]
rows.description: A toddler brings an empty katori to mother and taps it, saying "aur." Handing over the bowl says more than the word does.

rows.subtype: Approach: trial and error [Action]
rows.description: A toddler tugs at the kitchen cupboard where biscuits are kept, then at the fridge handle, then points at the counter. Each try shows what can be reached.

rows.subtype: Approach: frustration at a mismatch [Pitfall]
rows.description: A toddler wanted a biscuit and gets offered a banana. The toddler pushes it away and cries, because the goal was fixed on one thing and the request was not clear.

rows.subtype: Approach: accepting an alternative [Revision]
rows.description: After crying for a biscuit, a toddler sniffs, looks at the banana, and takes it. Hunger wins out, and the plan changes from getting a specific food to getting some food.
